query: A citizen was detained by the police for 48 hours without being presented before a magistrate. What are their constitutional rights?
answer: Under Article 22(2) of the Constitution of India and Section 58 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023, every person arrested and detained in custody must be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours of their arrest, excluding the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the magistrate's court. Detention beyond this 24-hour period without the authority of a magistrate is unlawful and constitutes a violation of fundamental rights, which may be challenged through a Writ of Habeas Corpus.

cited_articles.exact_quote: Every person who is arrested and detained in custody shall be produced before the nearest magistrate within a period of twenty-four hours of such arrest excluding the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the court of the magistrate and no such person shall be detained in custody beyond the said period without the authority of a magistrate.

No police officer shall detain in custody a person arrested without warrant for a longer period than under all the circumstances of the case is reasonable, and such period shall not, in the absence of a special order of a Magistrate under section 187, exceed twenty-four hours exclusive of the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the Magistrate's Court.

suggested_action: File a Writ Petition of Habeas Corpus before the High Court or Supreme Court immediately to challenge the unlawful detention and seek the production of the detainee before a magistrate.

query: Can a state university deny admission to a qualified applicant solely because of their religion or caste?
answer: No, a state university cannot deny admission to a qualified applicant solely on the grounds of religion, race, caste, or language. Article 29(2) of the Constitution of India explicitly mandates that no citizen shall be denied admission into any educational institution maintained by the State or receiving aid out of State funds on these grounds.

query: What are the direct remedies available in the Supreme Court for the enforcement of fundamental rights?
answer: Under Article 32 of the Constitution of India, citizens have the guaranteed right to move the Supreme Court for the enforcement of fundamental rights conferred by Part III. The Supreme Court is empowered to issue directions, orders, or writs, including those in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, and certiorari, to enforce these rights.

query: A consumer bought a brand new washing machine that malfunctioned immediately, and the dealer refused a refund or repair.
answer: Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, a 'consumer' is defined as a person who buys goods for consideration. A 'defect' refers to any fault or imperfection in the quality or standard of the goods. Since the washing machine malfunctioned immediately, it constitutes a defect. Section 39 of the CPA 2019 empowers the District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission to order the opposite party (the dealer/manufacturer) to remove the defect, replace the goods, or refund the price paid. Furthermore, under Section 82, a product liability action can be brought against a manufacturer or seller for harm caused by a defective product.

query: A 12-year-old child is being forced to work 10 hours a day in a firecracker manufacturing unit.
answer: The employment of a child below the age of fourteen years in any factory, mine, or hazardous employment is strictly prohibited under Article 24 of the Constitution of India. Furthermore, Article 39(e) and (f) mandate that the State direct its policy to ensure that the health and strength of children are not abused and that they are protected against exploitation and material abandonment. Forcing a 12-year-old to work in a firecracker unit, which is a hazardous environment, is a direct violation of these constitutional protections.

query: Can an individual approach the High Court under Article 226 if their civil rights are violated by a government municipal body?
answer: Yes, an individual can approach the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution of India. Article 226(1) empowers every High Court to issue directions, orders, or writs—including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, and certiorari—to any person or authority, including any Government, for the enforcement of rights conferred by Part III of the Constitution or for any other purpose. This power can be exercised by a High Court in relation to the territories within which the cause of action, wholly or in part, arises, even if the seat of the government or authority is outside those territories.

cited_articles.exact_quote: every High Court shall have power, throughout the territories in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction, to issue to any person or authority, including in appropriate cases, any Government, within those territories directions, orders or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, or any of them, for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III and for any other purpose.

The power conferred by clause (1) to issue directions, orders or writs to any Government, authority or person may also be exercised by any High Court exercising jurisdiction in relation to the territories within which the cause of action, wholly or in part, arises for the exercise of such power

This fundamental right imposes an obligation on the State to ensure access to education, which should not be denied based on administrative hurdles such as the lack of a birth certificate.
